title: Number System
tagline: Factors, HCF-LCM, remainders — the topic most exams underestimate.

subsections.title: Factors, LCM-HCF & Divisibility
subsections.trick: 1 is not prime — examiners plant this constantly in ‘how many prime factors’ questions. For ‘least number leaving remainder r with x, y, z’, always compute LCM(x,y,z) first and add r — never r first.

formulas.label: Least number leaving remainder r with x, y, z

pyqs.q: Find the least number which, when divided by 6, 9 and 15, leaves remainder 1 in each case.
pyqs.a: LCM(6,9,15) = 90, then add the common remainder: ×90+1 = 91 — always LCM first, remainder second, never the other way round.

subsections.title: Factors of a Composite Number
subsections.trick: Write N = aᵐ×bⁿ×cᵖ... first, always — every formula on this page is a one-line plug-in once you have the prime factorisation, so that's the only genuinely hard step.

pyqs.q: Find the total number of factors of 360, and how many are even.
pyqs.a: 360 = 2³×3²×5¹ → total factors = 4×3×2 = 24. For even factors, force the exponent of 2 to be ≥1 (3 choices: 1,2,3) and let 3's and 5's exponents range freely (3×2 choices) — direct count = 3×3×2 = ×18, no subtraction needed.

pyqs.q: A 3-digit number N has distinct non-zero digits, none a perfect square, and exactly one digit is prime. Find the number of factors of the minimum such N.
pyqs.a: Non-square digits available: {2,3,5,6,7,8}. Need exactly one prime digit (from {2,3,5,7}) and the rest composite (from {6,8}). To minimise N, take the smallest prime (2) plus both composites (6,8), arranged ascending: N=268=2²×67. Factors = (2+1)(1+1) = ×6.

pyqs.q: N = 2⁶×3⁵×5³×7². Find the number of divisors of the form (3r+1).
pyqs.a: A divisor ≡ 1 (mod 3) can't contain any factor of 3 (since 3≡0 mod 3 would poison it) — so first strip out the 3⁵ entirely and only combine powers of 2, 5, 7, then filter by residue mod 3 using each prime's own cycle. Works out to ×28 divisors.

subsections.title: Digit Sums & Remainder Theorems
subsections.trick: For 'sum of digits of a huge power expression', rewrite everything as a power of 10 times a small leftover factor — the power-of-10 part contributes nothing but trailing zeros, so only the leftover's digits matter. For 'remainder when aᵖ is divided by prime p', check Fermat's Little Theorem first: if gcd(a,p)=1, a^(p−1) mod p is always 1.

formulas.label: Divisibility by 11
formulas.latex: (\text{sum of digits, odd places}) - (\text{sum of digits, even places}) \equiv 0 \pmod{11}

pyqs.q: Find the remainder when 2¹⁰⁰ is divided by 101.
pyqs.a: 101 is prime and gcd(2,101)=1, and the exponent 100 is exactly p−1 — Fermat's Little Theorem gives the remainder as ×1 instantly, no computation at all.

pyqs.q: Find the sum of digits of N = 625⁶⁵ × 128³⁶.
pyqs.a: Rewrite as prime powers: (5⁴)⁶⁵×(2⁷)³⁶ = 5²⁶⁰×2²⁵² = (2×5)²⁵²×5⁸ = 10²⁵²×390625. The 10²⁵² just appends zeros — only 390625's digits matter: 3+9+0+6+2+5 = ×25.

pyqs.q: Find the sum of digits of (10⁵⁰+10²⁵−123).
pyqs.a: 10²⁵−123 = a block of 22 nines followed by 877 (borrowing cascades all the way down). Adding 10⁵⁰ just places a leading 1 far to the left with zeros in between — doesn't touch those digits. Sum = 1+(22×9)+8+7+7 = ×221.

pyqs.q: Find the sum of digits of the 4-digit number 4078.
pyqs.a: Straight addition: 4+0+7+8 = ×19 — a reminder that not every 'number properties' question needs a trick; sometimes it's just arithmetic.
